articles.title: Registration is now full for the 2024 ERP Boot Camp
articles.content:
The demand for the 2024 ERP Boot Camp was far beyond our expectations, and we reached our maximum registration of 30 people within one day. We already have a waiting list of over 30 people, so we have closed the registration site.

We realize that this is very disappointing to many people. We hope to offer another workshop like this next summer, or possibly earlier.

If you would like to get announcements about upcoming boot camps and webinars, you should join our email list.

You may also consider hosting a Mini ERP Boot Camp at your institution (in person or over Zoom).

articles.title: New Paper: Using Multivariate Pattern Analysis to Increase Effect Sizes for ERP Amplitude Comparisons
articles.content:
Carrasco, C. D., Bahle, B., Simmons, A. M., & Luck, S. J. (2024). Using multivariate pattern analysis to increase effect sizes for event-related potential analyses. Psychophysiology, 61, e14570. https://doi.org/10.1111/psyp.14570 [preprint]

Multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) can be used to “decode” subtle information from ERP signals, such as which of several faces a participant is perceiving or the orientation that someone is holding in working memory (see this previous blog post). This approach is so powerful that we started wondering whether it might also give us greater statistical power in more typical experiments where the goal is to determine whether an ERP component differs in amplitude across experimental conditions. For example, might we more easily be able to tell if N400 amplitude is different between two different classes of words by using decoding? If so, that might make it possible to detect effects that would otherwise be too small to be significant.

To address this question, we compared decoding with the conventional ERP analysis approach with using the 6 experimental paradigms in the ERP CORE. In the conventional ERP analysis, we measured the mean amplitude during the standard measurement window from each participant in the two conditions of the paradigm (e.g., faces versus cars for N170, deviants versus standards for MMN). We quantified the magnitude of the difference between conditions using Cohen’s dz (the variant of Cohen’s d corresponding to a paired t test). For example, the effect size in the conventional ERP comparison of faces versus cars in the N170 paradigm was approximately 1.7 (see the figure).

We also applied decoding to each paradigm. For example, in the N170 paradigm, we trained a support vector machine (SVM) to distinguish between ERPs elicited by faces and ERPs elicited by cars. This was done separately for each subject, and we converted the decoding accuracy into Cohen’s dz so that it could be compared with the dz from the conventional ERP analysis. As you can see from the bar labeled SVM in the figure above, the effect size for the SVM-based decoding analysis was almost twice as large as the effect size for the conventional ERP analysis. That’s a huge difference!

We found a similar benefit for SVM-based decoding over conventional ERP analyses in 7 of the 10 cases we tested (see the figure below). In the other 3 cases, the ERP and SVM effects were approximately equivalent. So, there doesn’t seem to be a downside to using decoding, at least in terms of effect size. But there can be a big benefit.

Because decoding has many possible benefits, we’ve added it into ERPLAB Toolbox. It’s super easy to use, and we’ve created detailed documentation and a video to explain how it works at a conceptual level and to show you how to use it.

We encourage you to apply it to your own data. It may give you the power to detect effects that are too small to be detected with conventional ERP analyses.

articles.title: A sparse neural code for acoustic targets enables speech-like vocal flexibility in parrots
articles.content: English speech flexibly recombines 44 phonemes into >20,000 words and limitless phrases. Here we identify a novel neural code supporting combinatorial vocal control in budgerigar parrots. Deep learning based acoustic analyses show that both English imitated and natural warble songs are composed of subsyllabic acoustic elements that are flexibly reused across acoustic contexts, analogous to phoneme reuse in words. Such reuse poses a scaling problem for songbird-inspired timing-based codes, which require distinct neural sequences for distinct syllables even when syllables share acoustic components. We identified neurons in the parrot frontal cortical nucleus MO that exhibit sparse bursts locked to reused acoustic elements independent of syllable identity, timing, or surrounding acoustic context. These results provide the first evidence for a sparse, acoustically-grounded vocal motor code that can be flexibly reused to assemble a large and combinatorial vocal repertoire.
articles.author: Zhao, Z., Plump, A. N., Jones, C., Teoh, H. K., Kardon, B., Goldberg, J. H.

articles.title: Activation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons promotes the attribution of incentive salience to reward cues in male rats
articles.content: Background: Reward-associated environmental stimuli (cues) can gain incentive salience in some individuals, thereby becoming attractive, reinforcing, and instigators of motivational states. In rodents, the tendency to attribute incentive salience can be measured using a Pavlovian Conditioned Approach (PavCA) procedure, in which approach to a food cue (sign-tracking), relative to approach to the food delivery location (goal-tracking) is the operational definition of the incentive salience attributed to the cue. Growing evidence suggests that acetylcholine promotes this process, thus the current study tested the effect of activating cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain on sign- and goal-tracking during PavCA. Methods: We injected a Cre-dependent virus with excitatory Designer Receptors Exclusively Activated by Designer Drugs (DREADDs) into the horizontal limb of the diagonal band of Broca of transgenic rats expressing cre-recombinase in acetylcholine containing neurons. We then injected clozapine-n-oxide (CNO) before each of eight sessions of PavCA. On the ninth session, no CNO was given to test if any effects were immediately reversible. Results: We found that activation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons increased sign-tracking over time without an overall effect on goal-tracking, relative to a control group injected with a control virus. Changes in responding from the final CNO session to the saline test did not differ between virus groups. Conclusions: This effect demonstrates that acetylcholine promotes the attribution of incentive salience to a reward-related cue. Future studies should investigate the effect of inhibiting this area on sign-tracking as well as how activation of this area influences reactivity to cues associated with other rewards such as drugs of abuse.
articles.author: Rakowski, E. A., King, C. P., Mukherjee, A., Holmes, E., Hannan, L., Loney, G. C., Meyer, P. J.

articles.title: Constricted pupil states index neural replay during wakeful rest in humans
articles.content: Neural replay has been linked to skill consolidation during wakeful rest, yet its physiological context in humans remains poorly understood. In animals, hippocampal ripples and associated replay occur more frequently within intrinsically oriented brain states associated with constricted pupils, suggesting that pupil dynamics may index neural replay events in humans. We combined magnetoencephalography-derived sequence replay with pupillometry in 25 participants learning a motor sequence across alternating intervals of practice and rest. Replay was indexed by smaller-pupil states, and replay timing clustered on the constricting phase of slow pupil fluctuations. More frequent replay accompanied larger cumulative offline gains during early learning, while smaller rest pupil was associated with better performance when practice resumed. Multivariate pupil features predicted replay-associated states across and within individuals while preceding pupil dynamics showed modest predictive ability to identify the precise onset of individual replay events. Here, we show that constricted-pupil states index neural replay during wakeful rest in humans, linking replay-associated physiology with early motor learning.
articles.author: Dash, D., Claudino, L., Sugata, H., Iwane, F., Cohen, L., Buch, E. R.

articles.title: Dopaminergic reward signals shape foraging decisions through learned value expectations
articles.content: A fundamental function of the nervous system is to direct animals towards life-sustaining resources and enable adaptive strategies for acquiring them. Foraging, the challenge of securing these resources from the environment, requires making decisions that balance local gains against costs, opening a window on value-based decision making in ecological context. Yet despite the centrality of foraging in life, the algorithms and neural mechanisms underlying foraging decisions are not well understood. We studied mice making stay-or-leave patch foraging decisions for water across poor- and rich-resource environments with dynamic local reward outcomes. We found that mice integrate immediate rewards, local reward history, and reward (i.e. value) expectations to guide foraging decisions, favoring greater time investment in rich-environment patches. Computational models revealed influence of a time-varying bias which mirrored the shape of a learned value function. Consistent with a reinforcement learning mechanism, dopamine in the ventral striatum signaled a temporal-difference reward prediction error, which could be used as a teaching signal to construct value functions, and calibrated optogenetic manipulation of dopamine to create fictive reward signals recapitulated the value-related decision bias. Taken together, our results shed new light on the neurocomputational basis of foraging, revealing a novel role for value expectations in dynamic environments. Further, they establish generalized function of biological reinforcement learning in ecological context, demonstrating a specific role for the canonical dopamine reward circuit in shaping temporally resolved value expectations to guide behavior and cognition. The unification of this framework with foraging opens a new avenue to elucidate principles of how animals learn and dynamically adjust cognitive strategies for real-world ecological problems.
